people.gloss: Owes no thanks (from the founder's saying: the fee is the whole of the thanks)
people.role: Head of Phất Y Cốc since 1090, sword cultivation and swordsmen for hire; the valley's one Wind root
people.appearance: A tall, quiet man in an old grey robe with one long sleeve, who stands sideways to everyone as if he were about to leave.
people.backstory: Thang Vô Tạ was a hawk-catcher's son on Thương Ưng Đài, the windy terrace of the Pivot's plateau, and the wind went into him there. He came to the valley at fifteen to sell a hawk and stayed for the sword. The second head Liễu Hành Vân (lieu_hanh_van) had kept the founder's grey robe and the Wind art folded into it closed for three centuries because no one had the Wind to open it; he had. He became head in 1090 and has hired out the valley's swords ever since, to the Pivot's war hall, the camel trains and the mines, by the founder's saying on the lintel. In 1130 the sword sage Tư Không Hạc Niên (tu_khong_hac_nien) sought him out, and the two fought on Cùng Mục Phong, forty days' ride from the valley, for three days (C186). The chronicle calls it a draw. He will not speak of it (A232), and his disciples climb the peak to read the sword marks. He has watched Lam Khế Ngôn (lam_khe_ngon) make the valley rich on her own terms and asked nothing, because a sword does not tell the contract house its business. Cửu Cao Phái takes the plateau's Wind children before he hears of most of them; in 1195 he rode out himself and reached Lộ Khinh Trần (lo_khinh_tran) a week ahead of its rider.
people.wants: To put the whole of the Brushed Sleeve Step into Lộ Khinh Trần before Cửu Cao can say the boy was theirs, and to keep the valley out of the Pivot's war with Thính Vũ.
people.secret: Since the winter of 1199 he has held the founder's robe open for Lộ Khinh Trần, whose breath of Wind is far under the bar the robe answers to, by lending each fold his own Wind. Each fold costs him what a season of seclusion would have given him, and the boy bleeds at the nose after it; Liêu Vọng Phong (lieu_vong_phong) holds the lamp at the hall door. And he lost on Cùng Mục Phong: on the third day Tư Không cut his left sleeve through and then lowered his sword, called it even and walked away without a sect, so that the valley would keep its head. The mended seam is under his arm.

people.gloss: A word given in a contract
people.role: Keeper of the contracts: she decides where the valley's swords are hired
people.appearance: A neat woman in a grey coat with ink on two fingers, who reads a client's hands before their letter.
people.backstory: Lam Khế Ngôn grew up among the camel drivers of Đà Đội Thôn, where her mother hired guards for the trains, and she came to the valley at sixteen with a better head for terms than for swords. Thang Vô Tạ (thang_vo_ta) took her as his first disciple and in 1147 gave her the valley's Contract Seal. She has made Phất Y rich: the Pivot's war hall pays a standing fee for forty swords, the mines of Ngọc Hành hire their guards from her, and the camel trains will not cross the steppe without a grey sleeve. She has never been on a long hire herself. In 1190 Thính Vũ Lâu offered three times the fee for a company on its southern iron road, on one condition: no Pivot line. She sealed it under a camel-train name (N-phat_y-03), and the Tower's money has paid for half the valley's new swords since. She plays go with the Pivot's drillmaster Đái Hổ Thần (dai_ho_than) when he comes to sign the year's contract.
people.wants: To keep the Tower's triple fee and the Pivot's standing fee both coming in, which means the war writ buried every spring, and to hire the valley's swords to anyone who pays, not only to the Pivot's friends.
people.secret: Since 1190 she has hired a company, under the name of a camel train of Đà Đội, to guard Thính Vũ Lâu's iron on the southern road, and she sealed it without the Pivot line: the only valley contract that would not end if the Pivot called. Nine of the company have died. She books each death on the Đà Đội camel road, has Giang Bích Sa write the train's stages and its dead into the road book and pays her a higher copying fee at every renewal, and pays Thôi Ấn Thư more for her silence each time a sleeve comes home.

people.backstory: Born at the horse-drinking spring of Mã Ẩm Tuyền, where the ground is warm in winter, she went out on her first hire at thirty and came back at fifty. She guarded the trains of the merchant Kim Vạn Lý (kim_van_ly) across the western plains, and he still owes her a year's pay. Thang Vô Tạ (thang_vo_ta) is her master. The swords of the valley would follow her before Lam Khế Ngôn (lam_khe_ngon), and both women know it. She does not know what the southern company's contract says, and has asked twice to ride south and see it kept.

He trusts the smiths and has noticed that Can Tương ore comes back as blades that ring more clearly than any star iron Hầu Thiết Anh (hau_thiet_anh) sells. He has not wondered why.

people.role: Founder of Phất Y Cốc (560, A225); a Wind-rooted hired sword who cut the valley's saying on its lintel
people.backstory: A wandering Wind-rooted swordsman who hired his sword for one deed at a time and took nothing past the fee. In 560 he settled the grassland valley under the Pivot, dug the ore of Can Tương for his students' swords (A225), and cut his saying on the lintel of the first hall: the fee is the whole of the thanks. In 790 he hung his grey robe in the hall, with his Wind art folded in the sleeve, and walked out. His disciple Liễu Hành Vân (lieu_hanh_van) kept the valley. He did not die then: on the ore road he took a ninety-year-old miner, Tư Không Hạc Niên (tu_khong_hac_nien), as his one disciple, gave him Cô Hạc, and was seen off from Tống Khách Thị in 900 (A138).
